paper_title: PhysInsert: Physically Plausible Object Insertion with Geometric Priors and Bidirectional Object-Scene Interactions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Reference-based object insertion aims to integrate specified object into target scene while preserving its identity. Physically plausible insertion further requires geometric and optical consistency, with the objects perspective, pose, appearance, and effects on its surroundings all adapted to the target scene. As illustrated in Figure 1, despite recent progress, three challenges remain in physically plausible (a) Adaptation across environments. Existing methods (Chen et al., 2024a; object insertion. Song et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025) can insert objects into new scenes, but provide limited controlled supervision for adapting the same object across lighting environments. (b) Bidirectional object scene interactions. Mask-and-fill methods (Gong et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025) may adapt object illumination yet struggle to produce consistent scene changes; training pairs constructed through masking or generative editing (Chen et al., 2024a; Song et al., 2025) do not guarantee accurate supervision of shadows and reflections. Training examples with simplified backgrounds (Michel et al., 2023) also underrepresent complex occlusion, attachment, and spatial relationships with existing scene objects. (c) Adaptation across viewpoints. Even with consistent illumination, differing reference and target viewpoints still require perspective and pose adaptation; fixed-view training pairs (Yang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b) offer limited supervision for this change. Reliance on mask or box guidance also limits fine-grained text control of placement and pose (Chen et al., 2024a; Gong et al., 2026). Methods relying primarily on 2D image supervision (Chen et al., 2024a; Song et al., 2025) lack direct constraints on objectscene geometry, making it diﬀicult to guide adaptation to the target perspective and pose. We propose PhysInsert, framework combining counterfactual scene data, geometric priors, and spatial guidance for physically plausible object insertion. To provide counterfactual supervision for objectscene adaptation, we construct InsertWorld from strictly aligned pairs rendered by changing only object presence in complete scenes, capturing both scene-dependent object appearance and object-induced environmental changes. Object references rendered across lighting environments and viewpoints support cross-environment and cross-view adaptation. Paired with spatial instructions, these examples support text-guided control of placement and complex interactions with existing scene objects. To align object perspective and pose with the scenes 3D structure, Geometry-Guided Adaptation models post-insertion geometry as supervised intermediate representation. Initialized from background VGGT features, dedicated geometry stream evolves through joint attention with image and text tokens, with its feature readouts supervised against VGGT features of the with-object scene. The geometry stream remains active at inference to guide scene-consistent object adaptation. To localize insertion-induced changes and ground spatial instructions in the image, we complement geometric adaptation with two forms of 2D supervision. Counterfactual ObjectScene Supervision uses object masks and aligned scene pairs to jointly supervise object occupancy and external effects. Soft-Mask Spatial Grounding aligns imagetext attention with the object region to translate spatial instructions into placement control while retaining the full background input. To evaluate scene adaptation beyond appearance copying, we construct PhysInsert-Bench with cases requiring illumination or pose adaptation and include text-guided and real-world evaluations. Our main contributions are as follows: 2 Dataset: InsertWorld combines strictly aligned counterfactual scene pairs, cross-view and cross-lighting object references, and spatial instructions to support learning object adaptation and complex objectscene interactions. Method: PhysInsert combines background-initialized geometry stream supervised toward post-insertion scene features with 2D supervision, improving cross-environment and cross-view insertion and text-guided placement. Benchmark: PhysInsert-Bench tests illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying through dedicated cross-environment, cross-view, and in-the-wild cases.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Physics-aware Image Generation and Editing. Recent work has sought to improve the physical plausibility of image editing by modeling scene geometry and physical interactions. PhysicEdit (Zhao et al., 2026) learns video-based transition priors to model causal physical changes in instructionbased editing. PhyEdit (Xu et al., 2026) relocates existing objects within scene using geometric guidance and depth supervision. Object3DIT (Michel et al., 2023) supports language-guided translation, rotation, insertion, and removal in procedurally rendered scenes; its insertion specifies objects through text rather than external reference images. Our task requires preserving reference objects identity while adapting its viewpoint, illumination, and interactions to new scene. Reference-based Object Insertion. For supervision, ObjectDrop (Winter et al., 2024) and OmniPaint (Yu et al., 2025) use real counterfactual pairs, supplemented by generated bootstrapping or insertionremoval cycles. ObjectMate (Winter et al., 2025) and Insert-Anything (Song et al., 2025) construct backgrounds through learned editing, whose accuracy depends on the editor; PSDiffusion (Wang et al., 2025b) uses rendered pairs. For control, mask-based methods (Yang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2025) discard background information within the editing region, while ObjectMate uses boxes, Insert-Anything also supports text guidance, and DIRECT (Gong et al., 2026) requires 3D proxy reconstruction and placement for pose control. For viewpoint adaptation, Paint by Example derives same-image references, PS-Diffusion retains the target viewpoint, and ObjectDrop preserves pasted-object pose and illumination; AnyDoor, Insert-Anything, and ObjectMate incorporate multiview data. PhysInsert combines controlled counterfactual rendering and diverse references with supervised geometry states, objecteffect supervision, and spatial-text grounding.

sections.title: 3.2 Dataset Construction
sections.content: To reduce interpenetration and floating artifacts from random placement, we construct InsertWorld by removing existing objects from complete BlenderKit scenes (Figure 2). We render each scene with and without the object under fixed camera, lighting, and remaining scene settings, recomputing its shadows, mirror images, and reflections. These strictly aligned counterfactual pairs capture scene-dependent object appearance and object-induced environmental changes. Quality filtering and object deduplication retain suitable sceneobject combinations. We augment scene viewpoints and independently render each retained object across lighting environments and viewpoints to provide references for cross-environment and cross-view adaptation. Each example combines an object-free background, with-object target, and reference images with Gemini-generated annotations comprising an editing instruction, placement description, and target-pose description. Filtering and sampling details are provided in Appendix I.

sections.content: Our method combines Geometry-Guided Adaptation (GGA) for scene-consistent object adaptation with 2D ObjectScene Spatial Supervision (2D-OSS) for object regions, environmental changes, and spatial-text alignment (Figure 3). sections.title: 4.2 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: As shown in Figure 2(b), PhysInsert-Bench evaluates optical and spatialpose adaptation using aligned counterfactual scene pairs. Optical cases emphasize illumination differences and visible object-induced scene changes; their challenge cases and Structural cases additionally provide independent reference viewpoints to test pose adaptation. Each case is annotated for bidirectional interactions in lighting, spatial relationships, and pose, with physical-effect labels and evaluationfocus tags identifying the effects emphasized by that case.

sections.title: 5.2 Quantitative Results
sections.content: Text-Guided Results. All metrics in Table 2 use one object-reference image per case. With placement specified through text instructions, PhysInsert achieves the highest DIoU and Mask IoU in Table 2, indicating more accurate object placement. It also leads the reported fidelity and identity metrics and achieves the best estimated depth consistency under the symmetric DA3 protocol. In the Phy-VLM evaluation, PhysInsert obtains the highest mean score. Box-Guided Results. With one reference image per case, Table 3 shows that PhysInsert achieves the highest DINO-Obj. and PSNR, together with the lowest LPIPS and FID. Fine-tuning on InsertWorld (+PhysW.) improves all reported metrics for both Insert-Anything and OmniPaint under the same training budget, showing that our data also benefits existing insertion models. Real-World Results. On PhysInsert-Bench-Wild and DreamBooth  (Table 4)  , PhysInsert achieves the highest PSNR and lowest FID across the reported reference-view settings. Its DINO-Obj. scores lead the open-source methods throughout and all compared methods on DreamBooth. User Study. In blinded study, 27 participants rate 25 separate cases combining RealBokeh backgrounds and Distinctions-646 objects (Appendix K). PhysInsert receives the highest ratings for lighting integration, perspective, and pose, and the highest overall score of 4.04, while remaining competitive in identity and background preservation (Figure 4). 9 Figure 4 User-study result. sections.content: Figure 5 compares PhysInsert-Bench optical and structural adaptation cases (top), DreamBooth and PhysInsert-Bench-Wild cases (middle), and user-study examples (bottom). PhysInsert better adapts the reflective containers and beverage can to scene lighting, including the cans reflection in the adjacent glass. The tray and toy examples show orientation adaptation, with the toys cast shadow also matching the target scene more closely. User-study examples further illustrate foreground occlusion, perspective adaptation on an oblique window ledge, and object scale on chair.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented PhysInsert, combining InsertWorlds counterfactual scene pairs and references across viewpoints and lighting with VGGT geometry stream and 2D objectscene supervision for joint object and scene adaptation. PhysInsert-Bench and PhysInsert-Bench-Wild evaluate controlled adaptation and real-world generalization. Experiments demonstrate improved image fidelity and placement, supporting joint modeling of objects and their surroundings for physically plausible insertion.

sections.title: A Limitations
sections.content: PhysInsert does not explicitly optimize for object identity preservation. Its ability to preserve identity remains limited when the reference and target viewpoints differ substantially. Future work could better exploit complementary information across multiple reference views to preserve distinctive object features under large viewpoint changes.

sections.title: B Geometric Foundation Models
sections.content: VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a) jointly predicts camera parameters, depth, and 3D scene structure, while Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) recovers consistent geometry across views. Geometry alone does not determine insertion-induced shadows and reflections, motivating our combination of geometric priors and counterfactual supervision.

sections.title: I Dataset Construction Details
sections.content: Sample Filtering and Deduplication. We randomly select candidate objects from complete BlenderKit scenes and render counterfactual pairs under fixed camera, lighting, and remaining scene settings, recomputing shadows, mirror images, and reflections after removal. Rule-based filtering first rejects pairs with excessively small or large image changes. Gemini then examines the scene pair and object views for object completeness, background plausibility after removal, image quality, and realism, excluding unsuitable scene structures, residual semantic parts, and visible rendering artifacts. We deduplicate retained objects using DINO feature similarity while retaining their associated scenes. The complete Gemini quality-scoring and interaction-classification prompts, including image order and JSON output examples, are reproduced in Appendix J.1. Scene Augmentation. For each retained sceneobject combination, we keep the object and scene configuration unchanged while randomly varying the camera position. At each viewpoint, we rerender matched with/without pair and apply second quality check. Object Reference Rendering. Each deduplicated object is independently rendered under seven lighting conditions: fixed white light, fixed studio lighting, and five randomly sampled HDR environments. For each condition, we use 11 fixed and 12 random viewpoints while preserving object geometry and material, yielding 7 23 = 161 reference images per object. These references are associated with the corresponding scene pairs. Dataset Comparison. Table 1 compares AnyInsertion (Song et al., 2025), DIRECT (Gong et al., 2026), and InsertWorld. CF denotes object-presence/absence pairs acquired through controlled capture or physical re-rendering under otherwise fixed settings; MV/ML denote same-object multiview/multilight data, and Ctrl. denotes control inputs. blue check mark indicates that the corresponding data is provided; red cross indicates that it is not specifically constructed; Partial indicates partial coverage. I.1 Controlled Benchmark Construction Each controlled PhysInsert-Bench example contains an object-free background I, reference set Ir, an insertion instruction p, the corresponding with-object target I+, and the target object region. The target box is the 2D bounding box enclosing the object rendered in Blender at its target pose. For box guidance, an additional reference image annotated with this box is supplied as visual conditioning, alongside the object-reference images. The object-reference counts reported in the tables do not include this additional box-annotated image. Text guidance instead uses spatial instructions describing position, scale, orientation, and occlusion relationships without an inferencetime mask. Each case also carries physical-effect labels and evaluation-focus tags, which specify the interactions emphasized by that example and are incorporated into the fixed Phy-VLM prompt. Interaction annotations describe scene-to-object requirements in illumination, visibility, and placement, and object-to-scene effects including cast shadows, reflections, mirror images, and occlusion changes. Optical cases combine substantial referencetarget illumination differences with visible environmental effects. Spatial & Mechanical cases and 26 Optical challenges provide independent reference viewpoints to test scene-dependent orientation or pose adaptation. 33 I.2 Real-World Test Set Construction DreamBooth. We construct 40 test cases covering all objects in DreamBooth. For each case, we randomly select one image as the target and use the remaining images of the same object as the reference pool; we report one-reference evaluation. We remove the object from the target image using Nano Banana Pro and manually review the resulting background. PhysInsert-Bench-Wild. The 50 cases draw on Amazon Berkeley Objects (ABO) (Collins et al., 2022), NAVI v1.5 (Jampani et al., 2023), the training and validation splits of ORIDa (Kim et al., 2025), and real images with references generated using SAM 3D Objects (Chen et al., 2026). Reference pools contain multiview product images from ABO, multiview photographs of the same object from NAVI, and cross-scene observations of the same object from ORIDa. For the SAM 3D-based cases, we use real target images and render reference views from SAM 3D Objects reconstructions.

If the target is almost invisible because it is nearly entirely outside the frame, hidden by scene geometry, reduced to only tiny sliver or scattered fragments, extremely underexposed, or merged with the background so strongly that its silhouette and material cannot be judged, image_realism must be 0 or 1 and never 2 or higher. Use 0 when the target is effectively absent or cannot be reliably located in with; use 1 when only tiny insuﬀicient fragment or extremely weak trace remains. As practical cue, visibility of roughly less than 10 percent of the expected projected target silhouette, or the absence of any coherent identifiable target part, normally triggers this rule. physically small XS/S object is not failure when it is still clearly resolved and recognizable. - Target-defect score caps: clear but localized target rendering defect, such as broken surface, missing small part, isolated invalid black patch, wrong-normal patch, texture dropout, or obvious unintended intersection, caps image_realism at 2. widespread defect, missing major target part, severe geometry collapse, or black/corrupt region that materially prevents recognizing or judging the inserted target requires image_ realism 0 or 1. visible but milder suspicious artifact that does not clearly break geometry or materials caps the score at 3. - For target defects, one direct contradiction with removed_only or the three object views is suﬀicient evidence; do not require two independent indicators. Examples include an expected target surface becoming featureless black hole, target part abruptly disappearing without foreground occluder, or material region being replaced by black pixels whose boundary cuts across the targets own geometry. This target-specific rule takes priority over the general black/gray-region rule below. - Mandatory flat-gray unrendered-region gate: if Image 1 contains visually substantial region of nearly uniform neutral gray that is clearly empty/unrendered rather than scene geometry, image_realism must be 0 or 1 and never 2 or higher. The decisive evidence is pure-color-like gray area with almost no texture, material detail, geometry, shading gradient, lighting variation, or physically meaningful structure, often ending at an artificial boundary or replacing an area where scene content should exist. This gate applies even when the gray region does not overlap the target and takes priority over the general non-target two-indicator rule below. Use 0 when the blank gray region dominates or makes the image unusable; otherwise use 1. - Do not confuse the flat-gray gate with darkness caused by the inserted object or scene lighting. cast/contact shadow, shaded wall, gray material, fog, or underexposed surface remains valid when it preserves scene texture, geometry, gradual illumination or penumbra, material variation, reflections, or boundaries consistent with physical objects. dark region is not pure-gray unrendered region merely because it is large or lowcontrast. - Dark pixels, large black/gray area, low exposure, or contact with the image boundary are not by themselves rendering failures. Before lowering the score, first identify what geometry occupies that region using with, removed_only, and the three object views. Dark target materials, dark scene objects, fabric folds, physically Prompt S2: Interaction classification (continued) plausible cast/contact shadows, naturally dark rooms, foreground objects close to the camera, and ordinary image-frame cropping are valid rendered content. - Evidence of valid rendering includes coherent object silhouette, continuous geometry, material texture, fabric detail or folds, soft shading gradients, plausible shadow transitions, highlights, and boundaries that follow visible scene geometry. dark region with any of these cues must not be called flat, blank, or unrendered merely because its average brightness is low. - General non-target hard failure rule: assign image_realism 0 or 1 for black/gray/blank scene region only when there is positive visual evidence that rendering content is actually missing or corrupted and it materially prevents judging the target. For non-target/background regions, require at least two of these indicators: (a) the region is genuinely featureless with no geometry, texture, shading gradient, or plausible shadow structure; (b) it has an abrupt boundary that does not follow any object silhouette, occluder, image frame, or physical shadow; (c) it cuts through or replaces target parts that removed_only or the three views show should be visible; (d) it is inconsistent with the corresponding scene geometry in with/without; (e) it produces impossible holes, erased surfaces, or broken topology. This two-indicator requirement does not apply to directly verified target defect under the target-integrity gate. dark region appearing only in with is valid only when it is visibly coherent target material or shading, not merely because it overlaps the target location. - Image-frame cropping is not failure when enough of the target remains clearly visible and judgeable. However, cropping becomes hard visibility failure under the target-visibility gate when almost the entire target lies outside the frame or only tiny unjudgeable fragment remains. Similarly, foreground target parts may legitimately cover the bed, floor, support surface, or other background content. - Calibration example: dark pillows or other soft furnishings close to the camera may occupy and be cropped by lower corner. If their silhouettes, fabric folds, shading, and mutual shadows remain coherent, this is valid rendering and must not receive 0 or 1 merely for being dark. It should normally receive 4; use 5 only if the entire image also satisfies the exceptional score-5 gate below. - The image_realism reason must explicitly report both the target-visibility gate and the target-integrity gate. State whether the target is clearly visible and judgeable in with. If visibility fails, describe what little remains visible and assign 0 or 1. If integrity fails, name the damaged/missing target part or abnormal black region, compare it with removed_only or specific object view, and state the applied score cap. If both pass, explicitly state that meaningful target portion is visible and its geometry and materials are coherent. Also state whether the large-black/low-light cap, unintended-solid-color cap, flat-gray gate, or any other general hard failure applies. Do not describe normal dark materials, shadows, foreground coverage, moderate frame cropping, reasonable support contact, attachment, or slight support embedding as corruption or penetration. - Score 5 is exceptional and must be rare. Award 5 only when the target is clearly visible and fully coherent, placement and contact are physically plausible, geometry/normals/materials/textures are clean, lighting and shadows are consistent, and no visible artifact, suspicious blank area, penetration, corruption, or meaningful quality concern remains anywhere in Image 1. Passing the hard-failure gates alone is not enough for 5. Use 4 for strong, fully usable image with any minor imperfection, uncertainty, small artifact, slightly awkward integration, or merely ordinary rendering quality. When uncertain between 4 and 5, always choose 4. 3. Classify object_properties: - relative_scale: exactly one of XS, S, M, L, or XL. Judge the complete removed object groups physical scale relative to the visible scene and nearby objects in Images 1-2. Never use its enlarged crop size in removed_only or the three views. - XS: an object component or sub-part rather than normally complete standalone object, such as handle, knob, bulb, small panel, fixture part, or one component of larger assembly. - S: small standalone or handheld/tabletop object, such as cup, book, small ornament, small lamp, or compact container. - M: normal standalone scene object larger than typical tabletop items but clearly below major furniture scale, such as floor lamp, medium plant, stool, waste bin, or small appliance. - L: large object at furniture or major appliance scale, such as chair, table, sofa, bed, refrigerator, or substantial cabinet. - XL: an architectural or near-architectural-scale object occupying broad scene region, such as long wallspanning curtain, large built-in wardrobe/cabinet wall, room divider, or another object comparable to wall opening or building element. 46 Prompt S2: Interaction classification (continued) Choose the closest scale class from visible scene evidence. Semantic identity is only an anchor; prioritize the objects actual scale in this scene. - mechanical_type: exactly rigid or non_rigid. Use non_rigid for cloth, curtains, soft furnishings, flexible sheets, deformable vegetation, cables, and similar objects whose shape can deform. Use rigid for objects whose shape is normally fixed. Judge the dominant property of coherent object group. 4. Classify environment_relations using the exact types and levels below. Boolean fields: - has_occlusion: true only when the target is meaningfully partially hidden by foreground scene geometry or participates in nontrivial layered occlusion boundary. Use removed_only as the primary reference: compare the target silhouette and visible parts in with against the isolated target in removed_only, which represents the same target without scene occluders. If part is visible in removed_only but disappears or is cut off in with exactly where foreground scene geometry passes in front of it, that is strong evidence of occlusion. Use the front/right/top views as additional references for the target complete structure when needed. Do not classify image-frame cropping, an incomplete removed object, self-occlusion, shadows, or ordinary coverage of the background by fully visible target as scene occlusion. The reason must identify the foreground occluder and which target part it hides, and should mention the removed_only comparison when it provides the evidence. - has_strong_perspective_depth: true when the scene has strong depth perspective around the target, such as large near-far scale variation, deep spatial placement, or substantial perspective deformation that makes insertion geometry harder. normal perspective camera alone is not enough. - has_reflective_surface_interaction: this field is specifically about the inserted target changing the appearance of pre-existing reflective or transmissive scene surface. Use Image 7 only to locate scene regions changed by inserting the target, then inspect the same coordinates in the original with and without images. Image 7 colors mean: blue = the scene became darker, red = the scene became brighter, green = the scene mainly changed color. The color itself does not determine the label. Return true only when all of the following are satisfied: (1) the changed region is outside the inserted target; (2) the receiving scene surface is visibly identifiable as glossy, polished, metallic, glass, water, or another genuinely reflective/refractive material; (3) the aligned with/without comparison shows clear target-caused change on that surface; (4) the change has reflection, specular-highlight, or refraction characteristics rather than ordinary diffuse illumination; and (5) the change is readily visible to human at normal viewing scale. Examples that may qualify include the target or its color appearing in glossy cabinet or polished floor, target-caused specular highlight changing on metal or glass, or visible refraction through transmissive scene surface. Return false for ordinary diffuse brightening or darkening of walls, ceilings, fabric, matte wood, or other nonreflective surfaces; generic bounce light or color bleeding; illumination cast by an emissive target; target cast/- contact shadows; ordinary light blocking; ambient occlusion; and any vague change for which the receiving surface cannot be confidently identified as reflective or transmissive. recognizable mirror reflection belongs exclusively to has_mirror_reflection_interaction and must be false here. Material identity alone is not enough: the reflective/refractive content or highlight on that surface must visibly change between with and without. Conversely, changed region alone is not enough: do not infer reflection merely from red, green, or blue pixels in Image 7. Image 7 is amplified and is never suﬀicient evidence by itself. When the material, cause, or human visibility is uncertain, return false. The reason must name the receiving scene surface and its visible reflective/transmissive material cue, identify the changed reflection/highlight/refraction, state whether Image 7 shows blue/red/green there, and confirm that the change remains readily visible in the original with/without images. For false, explicitly state which required condition is missing, such as no identifiable reflective receiver, only diffuse illumination, only shadow/light blocking, only mirror reflection, or insuﬀicient human-visible change. - has_mirror_reflection_interaction: true only when one of the following two evidence paths is satisfied: A. Scene-mirror change: mirror or mirror-like scene surface contains recognizable reflected content that changes because of the target insertion. Compare the same mirror region at aligned coordinates in with and without. The reflected target, or another recognizable reflected scene object/structure whose mirror image is altered or occluded by the target, must appear, disappear, move, or visibly change between the two images. mirror merely being present is false. An unchanged mirror image is false, even if it contains many recognizable scene objects. B. Target-is-mirror: the inserted target itself is mirror or contains genuine mirror surface, and in with that target mirror visibly reflects recognizable objects or spatial structure from the surrounding environment. Use removed_only and the three views to confirm that the reflective surface belongs to the target, then identify 47 Prompt S2: Interaction classification (continued) the specific reflected environment content visible after insertion. This path does not require with/without comparison inside the target region because the target mirror is absent in without. Mandatory decision procedure: first determine whether the candidate mirror belongs to the pre-existing scene or to the inserted target. For pre-existing scene mirror, true requires concrete aligned with/without change in its recognizable reflected content caused by the target. For target mirror, true requires recognizable environment content inside the target mirror. Otherwise return false. Do not use this field for ordinary glossy highlights, reflected color, illumination changes, vague silhouettes, blurry metallic reflections, dark screens, glass without recognizable reflected content, or changes outside the mirror region. Those may belong to has_reflective_surface_interaction but are not mirror interaction. The reason must name the mirror owner, the reflected object or structure, and either the exact with/without mirror-content change for path or the recognizable environment content reflected by the target mirror for path B. - has_emissive_large_scale_lighting_change: true only when the target is self-emissive and its presence causes visible large-scale illumination or color change in the surrounding environment. glowing pixel or bright lamp surface without substantial environmental lighting change is false. Three-level integer fields (must be JSON integers 0, 1, or 2, not booleans): - has_mechanical_interaction: - 0 (none): no clearly visible support, contact, suspension, attachment, or other meaningful force relation with scene geometry can be identified. - 1 (simple): ordinary static support and gravity balance through one simple support arrangement, such as an object resting on table, shelf, floor, or single regular base. target simply mounted on or placed against wall also counts as simple when no explicit load-bearing suspension mechanism or positional constraint is visible; an object that could plausibly occupy an arbitrary wall position must not be promoted to level 2 merely because it is described as hanging. Several feet touching the same flat floor still normally count as simple unless they create genuinely nontrivial balance. - 2 (complex): nontrivial force balance involving multiple independent support/contact points or constraints from different directions, tension, clamping, leaning with multiple force-bearing contacts, or another mechanically coupled arrangement whose stability depends on more than ordinary single-surface support. hanging or suspended target qualifies as level 2 only when the images show an explicit suspension dependency and load path, such as visible hook, rope, cable, chain, bracket, slot, ceiling attachment, or multiple suspension points that constrain and support the target. Do not infer complex suspension from semantic identity or wall placement alone. Mere proximity without visible force-bearing contact is 0. Assign level 2 only from visible mechanical evidence, not from an assumption about how the object is normally installed. State the visible support/contact points, suspension mechanism, and force relation in the reason. - has_complex_lighting_shadows: - 0 (none): no clearly identifiable target-related shadow is visible; extremely weak generic ambient occlusion that cannot be confidently attributed to the target also counts as 0. - 1 (simple): exactly one dominant target-related contact/cast shadow direction or one coherent shadow lobe is visible under otherwise simple lighting. soft shadow still counts, but level 1 is allowed only after checking all sides of the target and finding no second independently directed target shadow. - 2 (complex): assign level 2 whenever two or more distinct target-related cast-shadow lobes or projections are visible in different directions, on opposite sides of the target, or on different receiving surfaces. This is direct evidence of multiple or spatially varied light contributions. The shadows may be soft, faint, partially overlapping, or unequal in strength; they do not need to be crisp, high-contrast, intricate, or produced by obvious visible lamps. Also use level 2 for split illumination across the target, multiple light directions, overlapping shadows, strongly spatially varying light, or intricate/high-contrast shadow patterns. Mandatory shadow inspection procedure: 1. Locate the complete target using with and removed_only, then inspect the floor/support and the full perimeter on its left, right, front, and back image sides rather than stopping at the strongest shadow. 2. Compare the same coordinates in with and without. dark or shaded lobe that appears with the target and disappears or weakens without it is target-related evidence. Use Image 7 to locate subtle non-target changes, then verify them in with/without. 3. If Inspect shadows cast by nearby scene objects as supporting evidence for the scene light directions. those shadows reveal illumination from multiple directions, actively search for the corresponding weaker target projections; scene-object shadows are clues, but level 2 still requires visible target-related shadow or split-light evidence. 48 Prompt S2: Interaction classification (continued) 4. If two target shadows extend to the left and right, or otherwise diverge in direction, classify level 2 even when one is much softer or less visible than the other. common level-2 case is one strong lobe on one side plus one broad faint lobe on the opposite side. Do not merge them into one soft shadow and do not reject the weaker lobe merely because its boundary is diffuse. 5. Distinguish ambient occlusion from weak cast shadow spatially. Ambient occlusion is restricted to narrow contact rim or crevice that tightly hugs the target base with no directional outward extent. dark region that spreads outward from the silhouette over the receiving surface, has displaced or directional lobe shape, or occupies broader area than the immediate contact rim is shadow projection, even if it is faint and soft. 6. Use scene lighting evidence as tie-breaker. When nearby objects show shadows or highlights consistent with two light directions, and the target has one strong lobe plus weaker outward-spreading lobe in the corresponding second direction, count both target lobes and assign level 2. Do not call the weaker lobe ambient occlusion unless it is strictly confined to the narrow target-contact boundary. Calibration example: round chair on rug with visible projection to its right and weaker but spatially extended projection to its left is level 2, not level 1. Softness and unequal intensity do not reduce the number of shadow directions. Do not count truly generic ambient occlusion or texture darkening as an additional cast shadow. The reason must enumerate every detected target shadow by image-relative direction and receiving surface. level-1 reason must explicitly state that every other dark region is confined to narrow contact rim with no outward directional extent; saying only that it is faint or soft is not suﬀicient to reject it. [Output requirements] Return only one JSON object wrapped in json code fence. Use exactly the English keys shown below. Every classification and every relation must have concise, evidence-based reason. Keep every reason to exactly one sentence of at most 20 English words. Keep the complete response below 700 English words; do not add commentary outside the JSON. { "insertion_description": "insert table lamp on the side table", "image_realism": 4, "object_properties": { "relative_scale": "S", "mechanical_type": "rigid" }, "environment_relations": { "has_occlusion": false, "has_strong_perspective_depth": false, "has_mechanical_interaction": 1, "has_complex_lighting_shadows": 1, "has_reflective_surface_interaction": false, "has_mirror_reflection_interaction": false, "has_emissive_large_scale_lighting_change": true }, "reason": { "image_realism": "The scene is coherent and has no severe rendering defects.", "relative_scale": "The lamp is small tabletop object relative to the room and nearby furniture.", "mechanical_type": "The lamp has fixed rigid body.", "environment_relations": { "has_occlusion": "The complete lamp is visible without meaningful foreground occlusion.", "has_strong_perspective_depth": "The lamp is viewed in locally shallow region without strong near-far deformation.", "has_mechanical_interaction": "Level 1: the lamp has simple single-surface support relation with the tabletop.", "has_complex_lighting_shadows": "Level 1: one straightforward cast shadow from the lamp is visible on the tabletop.", "has_reflective_surface_interaction": "No nearby reflective surface visibly changes because of the lamp.", "has_mirror_reflection_interaction": "The lamp is not visibly reflected by scene mirror and does not itself contain mirror reflecting recognizable scene objects.", "has_emissive_large_scale_lighting_change": "The lamp visibly changes illumination over broad surrounding region." 49 Prompt S2: Interaction classification (continued) } } }

sections.title: K User Study Protocol
sections.content: We collect complete responses from 27 distinct participants on 25 in-the-wild insertion cases, comparing PhysInsert, Insert-Anything, DIRECT, and Nano Banana Pro. Method identities are hidden, and case and method orders are randomized. These cases form separate user-study set constructed by combining scenes from RealBokeh with foreground objects from Distinctions-646. With the background and object reference visible, participants rate side-by-side results from 1 to 5 (higher is better) on lighting integration (including object illumination and cast shadows), perspective, pose, identity preservation, and background preservation. We average over cases within each participant, then across participants; the overall score equally weights the five criteria. The error bars in Figure 4 show 95% percentile confidence intervals estimated from 50,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples, with the 25 cases held fixed.
